passage: The rasgulla tin was nearly empty on the kitchen counter of their Kolkata flat. Pallavi, five, lay on the floor kicking. "One more! Give it!" Her father, Uday, sat down on the floor beside her, not too close. "You're really angry, I can see that," he said evenly. "And no more sweets today." "You're mean!" He didn't answer that. He didn't call her a baby, and he didn't offer a biscuit instead. He just stayed. "When you want a hug, I'm right here." Pallavi kicked twice more, then slower.

qa.q: What did Uday say he would be there for?
qa.a: He said, "When you want a hug, I'm right here."

qa.q: Why might Pallavi's kicks be slowing at the end?
qa.a: His steady voice and staying close may be helping her feel safe enough to let the anger drain, even though she still wants the sweet.

qa.q: What makes Uday's response a turning point in the tantrum?
qa.a: He names her anger and keeps the no without shaming, bribing or shouting, and he stays available, so the storm can pass without the limit moving.

qa.q: What is Pallavi experiencing now that the limit isn't moving?
qa.a: She is still angry and calling him mean, but she is also finding out that her father stays near her even when she is at her worst.

grounding: Shows a father acknowledging his daughter's anger, holding the no on sweets without shame or bargaining, and staying available for comfort.

"I want more cake! Now!"
"You're so angry, Aadya. I hear it." Mridul crouched to her height.
"Give me Eshaan's piece then!"
"No more sweets today. That's the answer."
"You're a bad papa!"
Eshaan, nine, snorted. "She's being a baby."
"Eshaan, no names, please." Mridul turned back. "Still no cake, beta. I'm not cross with you."
Aadya howled and threw a cushion.
"I'll sit right here," he said, settling on the rug. "Come when you're ready."
The cushion landed near his knee. He left it there.

qa.q: How old is Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan is nine.

qa.q: What did Aadya want when she asked for Eshaan's piece?
qa.a: She was hoping to find a way around the no, trying a different route to get cake while she was still furious.

qa.q: How does Mridul handle Eshaan's comment, and why does it matter here?
qa.a: He stops the name-calling at once, so Aadya is not shamed while he holds the limit, keeping the focus on calm firmness.

qa.q: What might Eshaan be feeling while his sister howls?
qa.a: He may be irritated by the noise and protective of his own cake, and hearing Papa stop the name-calling shows him how anger is handled at home.

grounding: A father names his daughter's anger, keeps the no on sweets, blocks shaming, and waits nearby for her to come to him.

passage:
Parent diary note, Friday
At Diwali party pickup, Irfan's daughter asked for another kaju katli after the plate was packed away. When he said no, she lay on the classroom floor and yelled "I hate you!" Irfan crouched to her level and said, "I hear you are angry. The answer is still no more sweets today." No raised voice, no "naughty", no deal. He just stayed, one hand open on his knee. After a minute she crawled over to him. I put the sweet box out of sight in the staff room.
Saurabh, class teacher

qa.q: What did Irfan's daughter ask for?
qa.a: Another kaju katli after the plate was already packed away.

qa.q: How did Saurabh probably feel watching Irfan stay calm on the floor?
qa.a: Saurabh seems relieved and respectful, quietly helping by moving the sweet box rather than stepping in.

qa.q: Which part of Irfan's response worked, and why?
qa.a: He named her anger and kept the same no without shaming or bargaining, so she felt safe to come to him.

qa.q: What would change if Irfan had offered a deal to stop the yelling?
qa.a: His daughter might learn that lying on the floor and yelling can move the limit, making the next tantrum bigger.

grounding: Shows a teacher's note about a father who names his daughter's anger, keeps the limit on sweets, and stays available without shaming.

passage:
The kasba mithai shop was closing. Gurleen had already eaten her one peda from the paper bag.
"One more, Papa!"
"No, puttar."
"You're bad! I hate you!" She kicked the bicycle wheel and started to cry.
Manoj knelt on the dusty road so his eyes were level with hers. "I hear you are angry. The answer is still no more sweets today."
"But whyyy?"
He didn't argue the why or scold. He just stayed, arms open, and waited.
After a while Gurleen leaned into them, still sniffing.

qa.q: Where did Manoj kneel?
qa.a: On the dusty road, so his eyes were level with Gurleen's.

qa.q: Why did Manoj kneel so his eyes were level with Gurleen's?
qa.a: He wanted to stay calm and close rather than tower over her, showing he was steady and caring even while she was angry.

qa.q: What did Manoj do well at this stage?
qa.a: He kept the limit in calm words, did not scold or reargue the why, and kept his arms open for comfort.

qa.q: How is Gurleen likely experiencing her father's calm answer?
qa.a: It may feel frustrating at first, but also safe, because he stays close instead of shouting.

grounding: Shows a father in a small town calmly naming his daughter's anger, holding the no on sweets and staying available for comfort.

Gabriel from downstairs had brought a box of honey pastries, now empty. Selam wanted the biscuits on the top shelf instead.
"No more sweets today," Abebe said.
"I hate you! You're a mean daddy!"
Gabriel, still at the door, raised his eyebrows. Abebe didn't look at him. He sat on the rug. "I hear you are angry. The answer is still no more sweets today."
"I'm still angry!"
"That's okay. I'm right here." No lecture. He waited while the Toronto rain tapped the window.

qa.q: What did Gabriel bring?
qa.a: A box of honey pastries.

qa.q: Why might Selam still be shouting after Abebe's calm answer?
qa.a: She is still angry and disappointed about the biscuits, and her feeling takes time to settle even when the limit is kind.

qa.q: What could Abebe do next if Selam keeps shouting?
qa.a: Keep sitting nearby, say little, and offer a hug when she is ready, without adding a lecture or a new rule.

qa.q: How might Gabriel see Abebe's response from the doorway?
qa.a: Gabriel may be surprised at first and then impressed that Abebe stays calm and firm without looking for approval.

grounding: Shows a father abroad naming his daughter's anger, keeping the no on sweets and staying beside her without a lecture.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, a jar of toffees sat on the reception desk. Simran, five, had already had one from Baljeet at the counter. "Another! Papa, another!" Sumit shook his head. Simran's voice rose. "I hate you! Give it!" People looked up. Sumit crouched to her eye level and spoke low and steady. "I hear you're angry. The answer is still no more sweets today." He didn't bargain, didn't scold, didn't call her naughty. Simran howled and pushed his arm. He stayed, calm, arms open. "I'm right here when you want a hug."

qa.q: Who gave Simran her first toffee?
qa.a: Baljeet at the counter.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when she pushed Sumit's arm?
qa.a: She was angry and frustrated that the limit held, her big feelings still spilling over.

qa.q: Which parts of Sumit's response make the limit calm and firm?
qa.a: He crouched to her level, named her anger, repeated the no without bargaining, shaming or shouting, and stayed ready to hug.

qa.q: How might the people in the waiting room see Sumit?
qa.a: They may be surprised to see a parent stay so steady, and perhaps relieved there is no shouting match.

grounding: Shows a parent naming a child's anger while holding a firm no on sweets, without shaming, bargaining or shouting, and staying open for comfort.
